types.name: Layered process audit
types.note: A short check, at the place of work, that the standard is followed; each leadership layer asks its own questions.

types.name: Waste walk
types.note: Count the waste you see in one area: the eight wastes plus Mura and Muri.

layers.name: Team lead
layers.note: The team lead walks every day and checks the basics of the shift.

layers.name: Area manager
layers.note: The area manager walks every week and checks that the system around the shift works.

layers.name: Site lead
layers.note: The site lead walks every month and checks that the layers below close what they find.

team-lead.text: Everyone on the floor wears safety shoes and a hi-vis vest.
team-lead.standard: PPE rule at the gate: S3 shoes, vest on.

team-lead.text: Walkways and yellow lines are free of pallets and cages.

team-lead.standard: Training matrix: no solo work below level 2.

site-lead.text: Near misses were reported and discussed in the safety talk.

site-lead.text: The 5S score of the areas walked has not dropped since the last audit.
Each critical task is covered by at least two trained people per shift.
site-lead.standard: Skills matrix: two per critical task.

site-lead.text: The quality KPIs (mis-picks, damage) are on target or have a countermeasure.

safety.name: Safety
safety.meaning: A safety standard that slips once a day is a standard nobody believes in. The fix is visible leadership, not another poster.
moves: Stop the work the moment you see it and fix it with the person, not about the person.
Ask what makes the safe way harder than the unsafe one, and remove that.
Put the rule into the start-of-shift briefing for the next five days.
safety.question: What makes the unsafe way the easier way here?

standard.name: Standard work
standard.meaning: When the standard is not followed, the standard is often unclear, out of date or impossible in the time given. Check the standard before the people.
moves: Watch one cycle against the written standard and note every difference.
Rewrite the step with the people who do it and post the new version at the station.
Check the same question on the next three walks.
standard.question: Can the person show me the standard, and does it work in the time they have?

fives.name: Order and 5S
fives.meaning: Things out of place come back when they have no home, or when the home is in the wrong place. Give each item a home where it is used.
moves: Mark the home of the item that was out of place, with a label and a floor line.
Ask why it was parked there: no space, no time, or no rule?
Score the area in the 5S audit this week.
fives.question: Where would this have to live so that putting it back is the easy choice?

quality.name: Quality
quality.meaning: A quality check that is skipped lets the error travel to the customer. Find where the check is hard to do and make it part of the flow.
moves: Follow one error back to the step where it was made.
Make the check visible at that step: a shelf, a colour, a scan.
Count the errors daily for two weeks on the board.
quality.question: At which step could this error be caught the moment it happens?

visual.name: Visual management
visual.meaning: A board that is not current tells the team that nobody looks. When leaders use the board every day, the team keeps it up.
moves: Hold the next shift meeting at the board and ask about the red numbers.
Cut the board to the numbers someone acts on.
Give each red KPI one owner and one date, written on the board.
visual.question: Who looked at this board today, and what did they do because of it?

flow.name: Flow and handover
flow.meaning: Stock that piles up and handovers that get lost are signs that the steps are not linked. Limit what waits and make the handover a fixed moment.
moves: Mark a maximum on the floor and agree what happens when it is reached.
Fix the time and place of the handover and use one sheet.
Walk the flow from the waiting stock back to the step that sends it.
flow.question: What is waiting here, and who decides when it moves?

people.name: People and skills
people.meaning: A standard is only as strong as the training behind it. Gaps show up first with new people and in the tasks only one person can do.
moves: Check the skills matrix for the task and name the second person to train.
Pair the new starter with a buddy for the rest of the week.
Ask the leader to explain the standard; where they cannot, train the leader first.
people.question: If this person is off tomorrow, who does the task to the standard?

wastes.name: Transport
wastes.definition: Moving goods or paperwork more than the work needs.
wastes.example: Pallets moved twice: dock to buffer, buffer to rack.

wastes.name: Inventory
wastes.definition: More stock or work in progress than the next step needs.
wastes.example: Three hours of inbound waiting on the dock floor.

wastes.name: Motion
wastes.definition: People walking, bending or searching more than the task needs.
wastes.example: The packer walks 20 m to fetch tape every hour.

wastes.name: Waiting
wastes.definition: People or goods standing still while they wait for something.
wastes.example: Loaders wait for the truck; the truck waits for the paperwork.

wastes.name: Overproduction
wastes.definition: Making or preparing more, or earlier, than the customer needs.
wastes.example: Labels printed for the whole wave before the orders are final.

wastes.name: Over-processing
wastes.definition: Doing more to the product than the customer pays for.
wastes.example: Every parcel wrapped twice; a second scan nobody reads.

wastes.name: Defects
wastes.definition: Errors that need rework, a second check or a complaint.
wastes.example: Mis-picks found at packing and sent back to the aisle.

wastes.name: Unused skills
wastes.definition: Ideas and abilities of the team that nobody asks for.
wastes.example: The night shift knows a faster route; nobody wrote it down.

wastes.name: Mura (unevenness)
wastes.definition: Work that comes in peaks and troughs instead of an even flow.
wastes.example: 80 % of the trucks arrive between 6 and 8; the afternoon is empty.

wastes.name: Muri (overburden)
wastes.definition: People or machines pushed beyond a safe, sustainable load.
wastes.example: One person unloads a container alone at the end of a double shift.

tips: Stand where the work is done. Ask the person to show you, not to tell you.
Check the standard, not the person.
A “no” means the standard did not hold today. Ask what made it hard before you ask who.
Team leads daily, managers weekly, the site lead monthly. The higher layers check that the lower ones close their findings.
On a waste walk, tap + for every waste you see. The count shows where to look; the people show you why.
Every “no” you cannot fix on the spot becomes an action with an owner and a date, and the next walk checks it.
